text: Harness makers have three kinds of leather loops to choose from: hand made, patent and pressed.
Hand made loops are the best and are preferred on fine harness, but when well made they are too expensive for common work, and when poorly made they are inferior to the other kinds.
Patent loops are loops pressed up in hot dies and sold to the trade ready for use in every needed size and a variety of styles.
Pressed loops are loops made up in the workshop and shaped with dies and presses after they have been stitched on the straps.
Patent loops are nicely finished and much cheaper than hand made loops, so they have taken their place on medium grades and are also much used on common harness.
Hand made loops are more durable than other kinds and, because of how they are made, less uniform in style of creasing than loops made by dies.
Loop leather must be tempered in water to a condition where it is easily worked yet keeps the full impression of the creasing irons, which it will not do if either too wet or too dry.
The general rule for tempering loop leather is to soak it until thoroughly moistened, then remove it from the water and let it become surface dry before creasing.

Some workmen moisten the loop leather only a little before stitching it on and temper it afterwards with water and a sponge; leather found too dry after stitching can be corrected with a moist sponge.
For a well-shaped loop, a fulness of about three eighths of an inch over and above the width of the loop stick should be allowed for a one and one quarter inch loop of ordinary thickness.
The extra leather allowed in a loop must be worked up and outward to the corners; otherwise the corners will be thin and weak at the very point where the greatest strength is required.
Hand creased loops are commonly attached by stitching both sides before creasing.
Using a clamp together with the loop stick avoids much of the trouble of loop leather becoming too dry before it can be creased; with a clamp, an iron loop stick replaces the wooden one.
The back clamp iron is made the full length of the loop stick and one eighth of an inch wider, with an ear at each end projecting about one inch above the back iron and carrying a thumb screw.

With the back clamp iron, one side of the loop is stitched in place and the other inserted, then the thumb screws are tightened against the loop stick to hold everything until the loop is creased and finished, after which it is stitched fast.

When shaping a loop on an ordinary loop stick, first work up the sides with a slicker, then rub down the top, and keep working sides and top until the leather is pressed firmly against the stick, always working toward the corners to keep them full.

After a loop is worked up, the ends are trimmed true and the edge creases run with a hot creaser; then the pattern is traced off and outlined with a fine tickler before creasing up with suitable tools.
Creasing tools can be kept hot and clean by laying their ends on a metallic box heated by gas jets or an alcohol lamp, with the handles resting on a wire support.
The secret of success in creasing loops is to define all corners and outlines correctly before the leather becomes too hard to take an impression easily.

After the pattern on a loop is worked up, the loop stick is replaced by an iron one heated as hot as possible without burning, the leather is colored with iron and vinegar black, and the loop is worked over with warm creasers and slickers until perfectly dry.
If a hand made loop needs a better black, leave it until thoroughly seasoned, apply a slight coat of hatter's black, and when dry polish with a silk rag.
A loop that has been well worked is not improved by varnish of any kind.
A properly made loop is solid and free from grain cracks, with full, sharp corners and a well raised ornament; a soft loop is evidence of lack of skill or carelessness.
Pressed loops are the cheapest kind and, when well made, look nearly as good when new as the other styles.
Pressed loops are needled on, and the awl holes on the side last stitched can be placed so that they are almost invisible once the loop is pressed up.
The appliances for pressing loops are a good screw press, a metallic box with open ends, side plates, bottom plates, iron loop sticks, and top stamps or dies.
The metallic box for pressing loops has sides about 3 inches high inside and is 3 inches wide in the clear, except for cheek loops, which need a box wide enough to admit the winker.
The loop pressing box has two thumb screws in one side, about one and a half inches from the bottom, one within 2 inches of each end.
The side plates of the loop press must be screwed well up, or the heavy pressure on the top will make the loop spread on the top edge.
Two minutes under the press is all that is needed to make a firm pressed loop, even with cold irons.
After a pressed loop is seasoned, color it with vinegar and iron black, rub it with a woolen cloth when dry, and then finish it the same as a hand made loop.
